Class ClientAuthenticator

java.lang.Object
iu.oidc.provider.ClientAuthenticator
final class ClientAuthenticator extends Object
Authenticates a client at the token endpoint.

An endpoint may register more than one authorization record — to accept a credential being rotated in alongside the one it replaces, say — and what each record looks like decides which method it may accept, rather than the client naming one:

  • A RAW key whose kid is the client ID holds the client's secret. It answers client_secret_basic and client_secret_post by comparing the presented value, and client_secret_jwt by verifying a MAC the same secret keyed — which is why the secret is held as itself rather than as a digest of itself.
  • Any other key is an asymmetric one and answers private_key_jwt. When the registration also carries a revocation list it is a certificate authority, and the assertion's own x5c chain is verified against it; otherwise the registered key verifies the assertion directly.
  • A record with no key at all is an explicit public registration and answers none. Nothing is verified, so only a grant that proves possession by other means — an authorization code with PKCE — may be redeemed. This is distinct from an endpoint that registers no authorization at all, which accepts nothing.

Rejections are SecurityException, which a token endpoint answers as invalid_client. A fault that isn't the caller's — a defective registration, say — propagates as itself.

Which kind of verification a registration warrants is settled here; what does the verifying comes from the reference, since every implementation of IuPkiVerifier lives in a module this one has no business compiling against.

Nothing is held in memory across requests. A spent assertion is recorded in the deployment's data store rather than on this instance, so replay is refused across every node rather than only the one that verified the assertion.

  • Method Details

    • verifySecret

      static boolean verifySecret(edu.iu.crypt.WebKey jwk, String secret)
      Verifies a secret against the registered value.

      Compared through MessageDigest.isEqual(byte[], byte[]) rather than String.equals(Object): the comparison is the same, but it doesn't return early on the first differing byte, so how long a rejection takes says nothing about how much of the secret was right.

      Parameters:
      jwk - RAW key whose WebKey.getKey() is the registered secret
      secret - secret presented by the client
      Returns:
      true if the secret matches; else false
      Throws:
      IllegalStateException - if the registration carries no secret, which is a defective registration rather than a bad secret

    • authenticate

      ClientAuthenticator.Method authenticate(edu.iu.oidc.config.IuOidcClientEndpoint endpoint, String clientId, ClientAuthenticator.Credential credential)
      Authenticates a client against one registered endpoint.

      An endpoint may register more than one authorization record — to accept an old and a new credential during rotation, say. Each is tried in turn; the first that accepts the presented credential wins, and one match is all that's required. A record's failure doesn't refuse the client outright since a later record may still accept it, and if none does, the first failure is what's thrown, carrying every later one as suppressed — so a rejection reads as why the most likely record refused, without losing what the others said. An endpoint with no authorization at all — not even one record — refuses every credential and every public request.

      Parameters:
      endpoint - registered endpoint
      clientId - client ID the request named
      credential - credential presented, or null for a public client
      Returns:
      method that verified the credential
      Throws:
      SecurityException - if nothing registered accepts the credential
